name: Wei Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate the ore train at West Cut, a large mine, and lead the crew that loads the wagons below ground. I check couplings and brakes, then carry the ore along a narrow rail to the main lift. My two-year technical diploma helps when a fault light comes on, but the sound of a wheel often tells me first. I like an orderly train; the stale air and delays at the lift are tiring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are you planning around outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, with a partner, Lena, and grown children who have their own homes. I hope to stop full-time work at 65 if the figures allow it. My pay is ordinary for the role, and we have about four months of expenses saved, with some other mine jobs within reach. I use an AI assistant now and then to explain a manual, but I check its answer with the workshop book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the loading crew a faster report is welcome if it keeps the brake test visible. I would not make a grand speech about AI. An ordinary shift is worth more to me than a clever headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The train still needs an operator, and four months of expenses gives us breathing room. The lift has caused more missed production than software ever has. I would keep checking the assistant against the book, because a neat answer can still be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the train roster and sign the brake sheet myself each shift. I'd continue the monthly transfer into our retirement account at the current rate. In the first year I'd ask the workshop to show the crew which reports the new software actually saves time on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I can see the next few years of work and household bills clearly enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on the brake sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stop distance and pressure reading must match what I felt on the test run. I would mark any mismatch before loading a wagon. A report can be short, but the measurement cannot be skipped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI assistant more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a colleague shows me a useful example from our own equipment. I have no objection to it; I just do not trust a general answer over the workshop book. That is how I learned the current tool.

say: I would welcome **shorter reports** while keeping a visible brake test.
I would tell the crew an **ordinary shift** matters more than AI promises.
think: The **train role** looks steady and four months saved gives our household room.
I would still verify **AI answers** against the workshop book before acting.
do: Keep the **ore train roster** and sign the brake sheet each shift.
Continue **monthly retirement transfers** at our current rate during the first year.
S0.quote: A report can be short, but the measurement cannot be skipped.
fieldNote: He weighs **software usefulness** against a specific safety check rather than dismissing it outright.
His **moderate reserve** supports a planned retirement without making him wealthy.

steps.text: Keep operating the West Cut ore train and signing brake sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schedules and parts orders will change first, and the physical train may change later. I would ask to see a proven remote train on our rail before promising fewer drivers. The mine should show the crew the safety record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A control room could use fewer people to move ore, and my lead post might shrink. I can probably move to a nearby mine if necessary, but those places may test the same equipment. Four months of savings is a bridge, not a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving this year and spend one paid shift observing a remote train if West Cut offers a trial. I'd ask the supervisor for the trial's fault log before volunteering for any course. If my roster is cut, I'd apply for another ore train post at the two mines within driving distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still have choices, but I would count every change to my own shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the fault log need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for missed stops, brake faults and how quickly the controller responded. A clean demonstration is less useful than a month of messy runs. If those numbers are sound, I would try the console.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train at the first opportunity?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait for the first crew to finish the trial, then take a paid course if a post is available. I can learn a system that works; I dislike being the test case. There is still time in this picture.

say: I would ask for a **remote trial record** before anyone cuts train drivers.
I would distinguish **office planning** from physical rail work in this slower change.
think: My **lead roster** could shrink, and nearby mines may face the same equipment shift.
Our **four-month reserve** gives time to apply, but it cannot replace years of wages.
do: Observe a **paid train trial** this year if West Cut offers one.
Apply for **nearby rail posts** if my roster is cut.
feel: **Anxious** about my own shifts, with some room to respond.
S1.quote: A clean demonstration is less useful than a month of messy runs.
fieldNote: His **steady approach** requires a fault history before a control-room course.
He names **other mines** as a possible fallback without treating their vacancies as guaranteed.

steps.text: Observe a paid remote train trial if West Cut offers one
Apply for nearby ore train posts if West Cut cuts shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could write the train schedule and order parts, while capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. I would ask the mine to publish both staffing dates. Saying everything changes at once would only muddle the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the planning work changes and 63 when the robot date comes. If the train no longer needs me then, I would be two years short of the age I hoped to stop. Four months saved and some nearby mines give me options, but the pension figure might be much lower than we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the pension office this month for written figures at 63 and 65. I'd postpone replacing our car and put that monthly payment into a cash reserve. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for a manual rail vacancy if one is posted, and take a paid console course only if it leads to a named job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a pencil and a plan. The numbers may be tight, but I have enough time to check them before acting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would decide whether you retire at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I would compare the written pension estimate with our monthly bills. If it misses by too much, I would keep looking for work. I will not declare an early retirement from a rough guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why delay the car purchase?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The current car still runs and passes its inspection. A new payment would make a wage gap harder to cover. I can live with the worn seat for another year.

say: I would ask for **separate dates** for 2028 planning work and 2031 hands-on robots.
I would insist on **written staffing** information before telling the crew to retire or retrain.
think: At **63**, I might lose the train wage two years before my hoped-for stop.
Our **four-month cushion** buys decisions, but a lower pension could still hurt.
do: Postpone the **car replacement** and put its planned payment into cash savings.
Apply for a **manual rail vacancy** after 2028 if posted; train only for a named paid post.
feel: **Anxious** about income, while still able to make a plan.
S2.quote: I will not declare an early retirement from a rough guess.
fieldNote: He checks **pension figures** instead of treating early retirement as an automatic answer.
His **course condition** requires a paid path to a named post.
The **car delay** is a clear spending cut tied to a reserve transfer.

steps.text: Postpone replacing the family car this year
Put the planned car payment into cash savings each month
Apply for a posted manual rail vacancy after 2028
Take a paid console course if it leads to a named job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI by 2031 may take planning work when I am 63, with capable hands-on robots around 2034. That is after my hoped-for stop at 65. I would still want the mine to show how it plans to staff the train before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to build a bigger reserve and see whether my role shifts. I could finish at 65 if the train work lasts, but the planning part of leading may disappear at 63. I cannot count on two full years of lead pay without a roster promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add one hundred to our savings transfer every month from now, if our bills stay stable. I'd request a written train staffing plan this year and keep my current shifts. In the first year after 2031 I'd take a regular operator post if my lead duties end and the wage still covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The robot date is later, but the earlier roster decision is still on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a regular operator wage work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need the exact offer before saying yes. Lena and I can compare it with our housing and food costs. I would not pretend a title matters more than the monthly figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine offers remote training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the first group how the console performed over several months. If it works and a paid post is attached, I would take the course. I do not need to be first onto the ore train console to become a capable operator.

say: I would seek a **staffing plan** for 2031 before trusting the later 2034 robot date.
I would tell the crew **lead duties** may change before the train seat does.
think: I could reach **65** in the train if the roster holds.
A cut in **lead pay** at 63 would still disturb our planned last working years.
do: Add **one hundred monthly** to savings if household bills remain stable.
Request a **written roster** and take a bill-covering operator post if lead duties end.
feel: **Uneasy** about lead pay, with a plausible path to retirement.
S3.quote: I do not need to be first onto the ore train console to become a capable operator.
fieldNote: His **moderate savings** can grow over five years without assuming the company retains his role.
He tests a **lower-paid post** against actual household costs before accepting it.

steps.text: Add one hundred monthly to savings if bills stay stable
Keep operating the West Cut ore train this year
Take a regular operator post if offered at bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade should be enough for the mine to train younger staff on whatever equipment comes. AGI by 2036 could take planning work, and capable hands-on robots follow around 2039. I would ask for a yearly equipment plan and actual course places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036 and 71 around the robot date. If the pension figures work and my health holds, I hope to stop at 65. That puts my own train job outside those dates, although I would worry about my grown children finding steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue driving while I am fit and add one hundred a month to retirement savings this year if our budget allows. I'd ask for a written pension estimate at 65 and review it with Lena. In the first year after 2036, if I have retired, I'd help at the local workshop with basic brake checks twice a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own income if the pension is adequate. I would still watch how the younger crew are treated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the pension estimate falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether another year of work changes the figure enough. If not, Lena and I would look at our spending before making a decision. A later robot date does not pay our bills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help at the workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young mechanics have good hands, but some have never seen a loaded ore wagon stop. I can show the brake check without pretending I know their new software. It would keep me useful without a full shift.

say: I would ask for **annual plans** and course places before the 2036 and 2039 changes.
I would tell younger workers to practice **real brake checks** as equipment changes.
think: If I retire at **65**, both technology dates follow my own working years.
I still need the **pension estimate** to confirm our household income will be adequate.
do: Add **one hundred monthly** to retirement savings this year if our budget allows.
Keep the **train role** until retirement and review the written pension estimate with Lena.
feel: **Calm** about my own job if retirement figures hold.
S4.quote: A later robot date does not pay our bills now.
fieldNote: His **calm mood** depends on sufficient pension income, which he will verify rather than assume.
His **workshop plan** uses existing brake knowledge after retirement without claiming new employment.

steps.text: Add one hundred monthly to retirement savings if affordable
Keep operating the ore train until planned retirement if fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Planning work could change at 60 and the train seat could be at risk around 63, before I hope to stop at 65. A written roster, a paid path to another real post, and clear pension figures would help me choose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs the brake test when one person watches several trains. I can learn a console after it proves itself. I still want a named person responsible for the ore train's stopping distance.

headlineQuote: I still want a named person responsible for the ore train's stopping distance.
portrait: **Wei Bauer**, 58, leads an ore train loading crew at a large mine and notices mechanical faults early.
He has **typical pay**, about four months of expenses saved, a partner, grown children and some nearby mine options.
He uses **AI occasionally** for manuals, checks answers and adopts new tools after a real trial proves useful.
The **fastest AGI** timeline threatens his hoped-for stop at 65; longer timelines give more room for savings and pension checks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could threaten the train seat around 2031, two years before his hoped-for stop.
whatWouldHelp: A **written roster**, paid access to a real alternative post and clear pension figures would support his decision.
